repeats.answer: According to Reclamation's equipment-life studies, the average life of a Reclamation transformer is 40 years. This estimate is based on continuous operation at rated load and service conditions with an average ambient temperature of 40 °C (104 °F) and a temperature rise of 65 °C.

[Page 7] 1. PURPOSE 
This document is to provide guidance to Bureau of Reclamation (Reclamation) powerplant 
personnel in maintenance, diagnostics, and testing of transformers and associated 
equipment. 
2. INTRODUCTION TO RECLAMATION TRANSFORMERS 
Transformers rated 500 kilovoltamperes (kVA) and above are considered power 
transformers. Reclamation has hundreds of power transformers with voltages as low as 
480 volts (V) and as high as 550 kilovolts (kV). 
All generator step-up (GSU) transformers, and many station service, and excitation 
transformers are considered power transformers because they are rated 500 kVA or larger. 
Standards organizations such as American National Standards Institute/Institute of 
Electrical and Electronic Engineers (ANSI/IEEE) consider average GSU transformer life to 
be 20 to 25 years. This estimate is based on continuous operation at rated load and service 
conditions with an average ambient temperature of 40 °C (104 °F) and a temperature rise 
of 65 °C. This estimate is also based on the assumption that transformers receive adequate 
maintenance over their service life [24]. Reclamation, Bonneville Power Administration, 
and Western Area Power Administration conduct regular studies to determine statistical 
equipment life. These studies show that average life of a Reclamation transformer is 
40 years. Reclamation gets longer service than IEEE estimates because we operate at 
lower ambient temperatures and with lower loads. A significant number of transformers 
were purchased in the 1940s, 1950s, and into the 1970s. Several have been replaced, but

3. TRANSFORMER COOLING METHODS 
Heat is one of the most common destroyers of transformers. Operation at only 10 °C above 
the transformer rating will cut transformer life by 50%. Heat is caused by internal losses 
due to loading, high ambient temperature, and solar radiation. It is important to under­
stand how your particular transformers are cooled and how to detect problems in the 
cooling systems. ANSI and IEEE require the cooling class of each transformer to appear on 
its nameplate. Cooling classifications, with short explanations, appear in sections 3.1 and 
3.2. The letters of the class designate inside atmosphere and type or types of cooling. In 
some transformers, more than one class of cooling and load rating are indicated. At each

3.1 Dry Type Transformers 
Cooling classes of dry type transformers are covered by ANSI/IEEE standard 
C57.12.01 Section 5.1 [1]. A short explanation of each class is given below. 
1. Class AA are ventilated, self-cooled transformers. This means that there are 
ventilation ports located in outside walls of the transformer enclosure. There are no 
fans to force air into and out of the enclosure with typically no external fins or 
radiators. Cooler air enters the lower ports, is heated as it rises past windings, and 
exits the upper ventilation ports. (It will not be repeated below; but it is obvious that 
in every cooling class, some heat is also removed by natural circulation of air around 
the outside of the enclosure.) 
2. Class AFA transformers are self-cooled (A) and additionally cooled by forced 
circulation of air (FA). This means that there are ventilation ports for fan inlets and 
outlets only. (Inlets are usually filtered.) Normally, there are no additional 
ventilation ports for natural air circulation. 
3. Class AA/FA transformers are ventilated, self-cooled (same as Class AA in item 1). 
In addition, they have a fan or fans providing additional forced-air cooling. Fans may 
be wired to start automatically when the temperature reaches a pre-set

2. Class OW/A: Transformer coil and core are immersed in oil. This transformer 
has two ratings. Cooling for one rating (OW) is obtained as in 1 above. The self-

3.2.4 Liquid-Immersed, Forced Liquid-Cooled.  This category has two 
classes. 
1. Class FOA: Liquid-immersed, forced liquid-cooled with forced air-cooled. This 
transformer normally has only one rating. The transformer is cooled by pumping 
oil (forced oil) through a radiator normally attached to the outside of the tank. 
Also, air is forced by fans over the cooling surface. 
2. Class FOW: Liquid-immersed, forced liquid-cooled, water cooled. This 
transformer is cooled by an oil/water heat exchanger normally mounted separately 
from the tank. Both the transformer oil and the cooling water are pumped 
(forced) through the heat exchanger to accomplish cooling.

3. Class AA/FA transformers are ventilated, self-cooled (same as Class AA in item 1). 
In addition, they have a fan or fans providing additional forced-air cooling. Fans may 
be wired to start automatically when the temperature reaches a pre-set value. These 
transformers generally have a dual load rating, one for AA (self-cooling natural air 
flow) and a larger load rating for FA (forced air flow). 
4. Class ANV transformers are self-cooled (A), non-ventilated (NV) units. The 
enclosure has no ventilation ports or fans and is not sealed to exclude migration of 
outside air, but there are no provisions to intentionally allow outside air to enter and 
exit. Cooling is by natural circulation of air around the enclosure. This transformer 
may have some type of fins attached outside the enclosure to increase surface area for 
additional cooling. 
5. Class GA transformers are sealed with a gas inside (G) and are self-cooled (A). The 
enclosure is hermetically sealed to prevent leakage. These transformers typically have 
a gas, such as nitrogen or freon, to provide high dielectric and good heat removal. 
Cooling occurs by natural circulation of air around the outside of the enclosure. There 
are no fans to circulate cooling air; however, there may be fins attached to the outside 
to aid in cooling.

To ensure that moist air does not be pulled into a nitrogen-blanketed transformer, the nitrogen pressure should be added to bring the pressure to 2.5 to 3 psi. This is according to the manual, which states that "Add nitrogen to bring the pressure up to 2½ to 3 psi to insure that moist air will not be pulled in."

It's also important to note that the pressure should never go below about 1 psi during cold weather, and that the pressure gage should be checked regularly to ensure it is functioning properly. The manual recommends checking the pressure gage against the weekly data sheets, and that if the pressure never varies with seasonal temperature changes, the gage is defective.

According to the manual excerpts, if a radiator leak is welded with oil still inside, oil samples for dissolved gas analysis (DGA) should be taken before welding and 24 hours after re-energizing to identify any gas increases due to the welding process. This is crucial to ensure that the welding does not introduce additional gases into the oil that could affect the transformer's performance and safety.

The process is as follows:
1. **Before Welding**: Take an oil sample for DGA to establish a baseline reading.
2. **After Welding**: Wait 24 hours and then take another oil sample for DGA to detect any changes in gas content that might have occurred due to the welding.

This approach helps to identify any potential issues that could arise from the welding process and allows for timely maintenance or further investigation if necessary.

Leaks.  Tanks and radiators may develop oil leaks, especially at connections. To 
repair a leak in a radiator core, you must remove the radiator. Small leaks may 
also develop in headers or individual pipes. These small leaks possibly may be 
stopped by peening with a ball peen hammer. Some manufacturer’s field 
personnel try to stop leaks by using a two-part epoxy while the transformer is 
under vacuum. Do not try this unless the transformer has been drained, because 
a vacuum may cause bubbles to form in the oil that can lodge in the winding and 
cause arcing. When all else fails, the leak may be welded with oil still in the 
radiator, if proper precautions are carefully observed [3, 4]. Welding with oil 
inside will cause gases to form in the oil. Take an oil sample for a dissolved gas 
analysis (DGA) before welding and 24 hours after re-energizing to identify gas 
increases due to welding. If the leak is bad enough, the tank may have to be 
drained so the leak can be repaired. Treat leaks carefully; do not ignore them. Oil 
leaks are serious maintenance and environmental issues and should be corrected.

Water should not be sprayed on transformer radiators to increase cooling for several reasons:

**Mineral Deposits:** The manual explicitly warns against using water for cooling as it contains minerals that will deposit on the radiators as water evaporates. These deposits are difficult to remove and significantly reduce the efficiency of cooling.

**Alternative Methods:** The manual suggests using additional fans blowing on radiators and/or the transformer tank as a better alternative to spraying water.

**Potential for Damage:** Spraying water on transformers is generally discouraged due to the potential for damage. Water can enter the transformer in various forms, leading to issues with dielectric strength, sludge formation, and other problems.

**Maintenance and Environmental Concerns:** Water-related issues are considered serious maintenance and environmental problems. Leaks, for instance, require careful repair, and ignoring them can lead to more severe issues.

**Cleaning and Maintenance:** The manual recommends cleaning radiators with compressed air when they become dirty, rather than using water. This ensures efficient heat transfer to the cooling air, preventing temperature rise and maintaining transformer performance.

According to the manual, if you suspect a three-phase oil pump is running backwards, here's how to correct it:

**1. Reverse the Motor Phase Leads:**

The manual explicitly states:

* "Reverse two phase leads if this is encountered."

This is the primary method to correct reverse rotation.

**2. Check Oil Flow Indicators:**

* Regularly inspect the oil flow indicator, which has a small paddle that extends into the oil stream.
* Ensure the flow velocity is adequate (around 5 feet per second) to cause the paddle to rotate.
* If flow is low, a spring will return the paddle to the "off" position and trigger an alarm.

**3. Inspect Motor Load Current:**

* Use an ammeter to measure motor current on all three phases.
* Low motor load current compared to full load could indicate reverse rotation or low oil flow.

**4. Inspect Pump and Components:**

* Carefully inspect all valves to ensure they are fully open.
* Check for loose pump impellers on the shaft, sludge buildup, or debris in lines that might obstruct oil flow.
* Listen for unusual noises that could indicate issues like worn bearings or rubbing impellers.

**5. Test Fans:**

* Ensure all fans are operating correctly. If a fan is not running, investigate and repair it.

Remember to follow these steps systematically and make notes of your findings and observations. If the issue persists after these measures, further investigation by a qualified technician may be necessary.

Based on the manual excerpts, here is the answer to your question:

A dial thermometer should be tested against a mercury thermometer every 3 to 5 years, or if trouble is suspected. The test involves suspending the dial thermometer's indicator bulb and a mercury thermometer in an oil bath, ensuring they don't touch the container's sides or bottom. Heat the oil while stirring and compare the temperatures, paying particular attention to the upper temperature range of your transformers (50°C to 80°C).

If the dial thermometer differs by more than 5°C from the mercury thermometer, it should be replaced. Keep a number of spares on hand, based on the number of transformers at your plant.

The manual mentions that oil bath test kits are available from the Qualitrol Company (716-586-1515) for shipping defective dial thermometers for repair and calibration.

Field testing has shown that out-of-calibration transformer temperature gages can read 15 °C to 20 °C lower than the actual temperature. This is a significant issue because it can lead to transformers running hotter than intended, which can shorten their service life or cause premature failure. The manual recommends replacing such gages and emphasizes the importance of accurate temperature readings for transformer maintenance and loading operations.

Additionally, the manual provides instructions for testing and replacing temperature gages every 3 to 5 years or when trouble is suspected. The testing procedure involves suspending the dial indicator and a mercury thermometer in an oil bath and comparing their temperatures as the oil is heated.

repeats.answer:
If the bottom contacts of a Buchholz relay activate during operation, it means that the oil level is very low, or a pressure wave has activated. If this relay operates, do not re-energize the transformer until you have determined the exact cause.

On the other hand, if the top contacts of a Buchholz relay activate during operation, it means that the transformer is gassing. If this relay operates, do not re-energize the transformer until you have determined the exact cause.

Here's a breakdown of what these conditions indicate:

**Bottom Contacts Activation:**

* **Low Oil Level:** The bottom float and relay are designed to be activated only when the oil level falls significantly low, typically when the conservator is almost empty. This indicates a potential problem with the transformer's cooling system or a loss of oil.
* **Pressure Wave:** A pressure wave in the oil, often caused by a fault within the transformer, can also trigger the bottom contacts. This pressure wave displaces the bottom float, activating the relay.

**Top Contacts Activation:**

* **Transformer Gassing:** When the top contacts activate, it signifies that gas is accumulating in the transformer's tank. This gas buildup is a sign of trouble, often related to overheating, eddy currents, or partial discharges within the transformer.

Remember, in both cases, it's crucial to investigate the cause of the relay activation before re-energizing the transformer.

4.7 Transformer Testing 
When the transformer is new before energizing and every 3 to 5 years, the 
transformer and bushings should be Doble tested.  Transformer testing falls into 
three broad categories: Factory testing when the transformer is new or has been 
refurbished, acceptance testing upon delivery, and field testing for maintenance and 
diagnostic purposes. Some tests at the factory are common to most power 
transformers, but many of the factory tests are transformer- specific. Table 17 lists 
several tests. This test chart has been adapted from IEEE 62-1995 reference [19]. Not 
all of the listed tests are done at the factory, and not all of them are done in the field. 
Each transformer and each situation is different, requiring its own unique approach 
and tests. 
Details of how to run specific tests will not be addressed in this FIST. It would be 
impractical to repeat how to do Doble testing of a transformer when the information is 
readily available in Doble publications. With some exceptions, this is true for most of 
the tests. Specific information is readily available within the test instrument 
manufacturers literature. Another example is the transformer turns ratio test (TTR); 
specific test information is available with the instrument. However, information on 
some tests may not be available and will be covered briefly.

4.2 Oil Preservation Sealing Systems 
The purpose of sealing systems is to prevent air and moisture from contaminating oil 
and cellulose insulation. Sealing systems are designed to prevent oil inside the 
transformer from coming into contact with air. Air contains moisture, which causes 
sludging and an abundant supply of oxygen. Oxygen in combination with moisture 
causes greatly accelerated deterioration of the cellulose. This oxygen-moisture 
combination will greatly reduce service life of the transformer.

The recommended minimum pipe size between a conservator's air dryer and the conservator is ¾- to 1-inch piping. If the pipe size is too small, a vacuum will appear in the transformer, which can lead to several issues:

* **Bubbles in the oil:** Insufficient air intake can cause bubbles to form in the oil, as the oil and air cannot be effectively separated.
* **Gas detector relay activation:** Small pipe sizes can result in a vacuum, which may trigger gas detector relays like the Buchholz and/or bladder failure relay.
* **Air intake around gaskets:** The vacuum can pull in air around gaskets that are not tight enough, potentially leading to further issues.

This situation is particularly common with transformers that are frequently in and out of service and located in areas with large temperature variations.

repeats.answer: A new bladder failure relay alarms one month after the transformer is put into service. While it is possible that the bladder has failed, it is not definitive without further investigation. The manual suggests that it is common for some air or gas to be entrapped in the transformer and piping when new, and it takes a while for this air to rise and activate the relay. Therefore, if the alarm activates within 2 to 3 months after the transformer is put into operation, it is recommended to recomission the relay with pressure or vacuum. If no more alarms occur, the bladder is likely intact. If alarms continue, further investigation is required, including checking for oil leaks in the conservator and transformer, and analyzing the dissolved gas analysis (DGA) to detect any gas accumulation.

The manual states that if the gasket is ¼-inch thick, it should be compressed to about 43 to 45% of its original thickness. This means that the final thickness of the gasket after compression should be:

* 0.43 x 0.25 = 0.108 inches (43% of ¼-inch)
* 0.45 x 0.25 = 0.1125 inches (45% of ¼-inch)

So, the gasket should be compressed to approximately 0.108 to 0.1125 inches thick.

* **Table 2** (Page 37) provides recommended gasket thicknesses for circular nitrile gaskets based on groove depth. For a groove 1/4 inch deep, a gasket thickness of **1/16 inch** is recommended.

**Additional Tips:**

* Always cut the outer diameter first and the inner diameter second, subtracting 1/4 inch from the outer diameter and adding it to the inner diameter.

To determine how much of the groove width a nitrile gasket's cross section should fill, follow these steps:

1. **Determine the Groove Width:** The groove width is equal to the outer diameter (OD) minus the inner diameter (ID) divided by two:
   OD - ID

2. **Calculate the Expansion Space:** For nitrile, the amount of horizontal room needed is about 15 to 25%. Therefore, subtract this percentage from 100% to determine the percentage of the groove width that the gasket should fill:
   100% - 15% to 25% = 75% to 85%

3. **Example Calculation:** For a groove with an outer diameter (OD) of 8 inches and an inner diameter (ID) of 6 inches:
   OD - ID = 8 - 6 = 2 inches
   Groove width = 2 inches
   Expansion space = 25% of 1 inch = 0.25 inches
   Gasket width = 75% of 1 inch = 0.75 inches

4. **Cut the Gasket Cross Section:** Always cut the outer diameter first. Subtract the expansion space from the outer diameter to determine the outer diameter of the gasket:
   8 inches - 0.25 inches = 7.75 inches
   Then, add the expansion space to the inner diameter to determine the inner diameter of the gasket:
   6 inches + 0.25 inches = 6.25 inches

5. **Check the Gasket Width:** Subtract the inner radius from the outer radius to make sure you get the correct gasket width:
   3.75 inches (outer radius, ½ of 7.75) - 3.125 inches (inner radius, ½ of 6.25) = 0.625 inches, which is close to the calculated gasket width of 0.75 inches.

Therefore, the nitrile gasket's cross section should fill about 75% to 85% of the groove width, with the expansion space being equally distributed on both sides of the gasket.

To join the ends of nitrile ribbon, the ends should be cut at an angle (scarfed) at approximately 15 degrees. The length of the angle cut should be about four times the thickness of the gasket.

For example, if the gasket thickness is 1/16 inch (0.0625 inches), the cut should be approximately 1/2 inch long. For a gasket thickness of 1/8 inch (0.125 inches), the cut should be about 0.5 inches long.

A jig or template can be used to hold the gasket at a 15-degree angle while cutting and sanding to ensure precision.

For older bushings with 15 kV and above ratings that require a semiconductive gasket and similar gasket material is not available, you can use cork-neoprene as a replacement. Additionally, thin metal conductive shim stock can be folded over the outer perimeter around approximately one-half the circumference to provide a semiconductive path. Here are the steps:

1. **Prepare Cork-Neoprene Gasket:** If cork-neoprene is the chosen replacement, ensure it is properly compressed and fits the joint design. Cork-nitrile is preferred for its better performance at higher temperatures and easier conformity to mating surfaces.

2. **Use Conductive Shim Stock:** As an alternative, thin metal conductive shim stock can be folded over the outer perimeter around about one-half the circumference of the gasket. These pieces should be evenly spaced and long enough to be held when the bolts are tightened.

3. **Install the Gasket:** Carefully install the chosen gasket or shim stock around the bottom porcelain skirt flange, ensuring it is properly sized to avoid forcing the rubber into the metal-to-metal contact area, which could lead to leaks.

4. **Ensure Semiconductive Path:** If using the conductive shim stock, make sure it provides a semiconductive path to ground, allowing static electric charges to bleed off.

5. **Apply Sealant (Optional):** Consider using a sealant like Loctite "Hi-tack" or GE glyptol No. 1201B-red to further secure the gasket and metal surfaces. Ensure the temperature is above 70 °F for optimal paint curing.

Transformer oils serve the following essential functions:

1. **Insulation**: Transformer oils act as an electrical insulator, preventing direct contact between conductive parts and ensuring proper operation without short circuits.

2. **Cooling**: They help dissipate heat generated during the operation of the transformer, keeping the transformer's temperature within safe limits.

3. **Arc Extinction**: Transformer oils facilitate the extinction of electrical arcs, which can occur due to faults in the system. This prevents damage to the transformer and potential fires.

4. **Dissolution of Gases**: The oil dissolves gases produced by the degradation of the oil itself, moisture, and gas from cellulose insulation. This is crucial for maintaining the transformer's health, as these dissolved gases provide valuable insights into the transformer's condition.

5. **Health Monitoring**: Regular dissolved gas analysis (DGA) is recommended to monitor the dissolved gases in the oil. This analysis provides critical information about the transformer's health, allowing for early detection of potential issues.

4.4.1 Transformer Oil Functions.  Transformer oils perform at least four 
functions for the transformer. Oil provides insulation, provides cooling, and helps

the oil, and other oil properties, provides the most valuable information about 
transformer health. Looking for trends by comparing information provided in 
several DGAs, and understanding its meaning, is the most important transformer 
diagnostic tool.

year, and more often if a problem is encountered, do a DGA. This is by far the

A dissolved gas analysis (DGA) is unreliable under the following conditions:

**Significantly Increasing Gases:** If the total dissolved combustible gas (TDCG) and individual gas concentrations are increasing significantly (more than 30 ppm/day), it indicates an active fault or high-energy arc. In this case, the transformer should be de-energized and further investigation is required.

**High Energy Arcing:** A significant presence of acetylene (C2H2) in the DGA indicates high-energy arcing. Even trace amounts of acetylene can be generated by a thermal fault at 500°C. This situation requires weekly oil samples to determine if additional acetylene is being produced.

**Excessive Decomposition:** A TDCG within the range of 1,941-2,630 ppm or individual gas concentrations exceeding specified levels in Table 4 indicate excessive decomposition of cellulose insulation and/or oil. This condition requires extreme caution, and further analysis is necessary.

**Load Dependence:** If the gas generation rate is found to be dependent on the load, it suggests potential overloading. In such cases, oil samples should be taken every time the load changes, but frequent load changes might make this impractical.

**Previous DGA Tests:** If previous DGA tests exist, they should be reviewed to assess the stability of the transformer's gas concentrations. Significant increases in gases compared to previous data indicate an unstable situation.

The manual emphasizes that DGA results should be interpreted carefully, considering individual gas concentrations, TDCG generation rates, and load dependencies. Transformers with unreliable DGA results should be taken out of service and further investigated to prevent potential failures.

The dissolved gases that come from the degradation of the cellulose (paper) insulation rather than the oil are:

- Carbon dioxide (CO2)
- Oxygen (O2)
- Nitrogen (N2)
- Moisture

These gases can also be absorbed from the air if there is an oil/air interface or a leak in the tank. According to the manual, these gases are formed from the degradation of cellulose (paper) insulation and are not produced by the degradation of the oil itself, except for carbon monoxide (CO) and oxygen (O2).
repeats.context:
[Page 43] Key gases 
formed by degradation of oil and paper insulation are hydrogen (H2), methane 
(CH4), ethane (C2 H6), ethylene (C2 H4), acetylene (C2 H2), carbon monoxide (CO), 
and oxygen (O2). Except for carbon monoxide and oxygen, all these gases are 
formed from the degradation of the oil itself. Carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide 
(CO2), and oxygen are formed from degradation of cellulose (paper) insulation. 
Carbon dioxide, oxygen, nitrogen (N2 ), and moisture can also be absorbed from the 
air if there is a oil/air interface, or if there is a leak in the tank. Some of our 
transformers have a pressurized nitrogen blanket above the oil and, in these 
cases, nitrogen may be near saturation.  (See table 4.) Gas type and amounts are 
determined by where the fault occurs in the transformer and the severity and 
energy of the event. Events range from low energy events such as partial 
discharge, which produces hydrogen and trace amounts of methane and ethane, to 
very high energy sustained arcing, capable of generating all the gases including 
acetylene, which requires the most energy.

The guide uses combinations of individual gases and total combustible gas

used to evaluate transformers. The four conditions are defined below:

exposed to air during sampling or handling at the lab. If a fault is suspected, look 
carefully to see if CO is increasing. If CO is increasing around 70 ppm or more per 
month (generation limit from IEC 60599), there is probably a fault. It is a good

4.4 Transformer Oils 
4.4.1 Transformer Oil Functions.  Transformer oils perform at least four 
functions for the transformer. Oil provides insulation, provides cooling, and helps 
extinguish arcs. Oil also dissolves gases generated by oil degradation, moisture 
and gas from cellulose insulation, deterioration, and gases and moisture from 
whatever atmosphere the oil is exposed to. Close observation of dissolved gases in 
the oil, and other oil properties, provides the most valuable information about 
transformer health. Looking for trends by comparing information provided in 
several DGAs, and understanding its meaning, is the most important transformer 
diagnostic tool. 
4.4.2 Dissolved Gas Analysis. After 1 month of service and once each 
year, and more often if a problem is encountered, do a DGA. This is by far the 
most important tool for determining the health of a transformer.

If acetylene is detected in the Dissolved Gas Analysis (DGA), the manual suggests taking oil samples weekly to monitor the acetylene generation rate. This is because acetylene indicates high-energy arcing, and frequent monitoring can help determine if the transformer is experiencing an ongoing fault. The manual also emphasizes that even a small amount of acetylene above a few ppm can be a significant indicator of a high-energy arc fault.

Additionally, the manual mentions that if the acetylene level is below the IEEE Condition 4 but continues to increase, the transformer should still be taken out of service to prevent further damage.

The sampling frequency is also influenced by the overall DGA values and the transformer's condition. If other gas generation rates exceed the G1 limits (10% of L1 limits per month), the manual recommends reducing the DGA sample interval and taking more frequent samples to closely monitor the situation.

[Page 72] 4.6.7 Taking Oil Samples for DGA.  Sampling procedures and lab handling are 
usually areas that cause the most problems in getting an accurate DGA. There 
are times when atmospheric gases, moisture, or hydrogen take a sudden leap from 
one DGA to the next. As has been mentioned, at these times, one should 
immediately take another sample to confirm DGA values. It is, of course, possible 
that the transformer has developed an atmospheric leak, or that a fault has 
suddenly occurred inside. More often, the sample has not been taken properly, or 
it has been contaminated with atmospheric gases or mishandled in other ways. 
The sample must be protected from all contamination, including atmospheric 
exposure. 
Do not take samples from the small sample ports located on the side of the large 
sample (drain) valves. These ports are too small to adequately flush the large 
valve and pipe nipple connected to the tank; in addition, air can be drawn past the 
threads and contaminate the sample. Fluid in the valve and pipe nipple remain 
dormant during operation and can be contaminated with moisture, microscopic 
stem packing particles, and other particles. The volume of oil in this location can 
also be contaminated with gases, especially hydrogen. Hydrogen is one of the 
easiest gasses to form. With hot sun on the side of the transformer tank where 
the sample valve is located, high ambient temperature, high oil temperature, and 
captured oil in the sample valve and extension, hydrogen formed will stay in this 

[Page 81] If both L1 limits and G1 limits are exceeded, we should become more concerned. 
Reduce sampling intervals, get outside advice, reduce loading, check transformer 
cooling and oil levels, etc.  If G2 generation limits are exceeded, we should 
be extremely concerned.  It will not be long before L3 limits are exceeded, and 
consideration must be given to removing the transformer from service, for testing, 
repair, or replacement. 
If acetylene is being generated, the transformer should be taken out of 
service.  However as with mineral oil transformers, a one-time nearby lightning 
strike or through fault can cause a “one-time” generation of acetylene. If you 
notice acetylene in the DGA, immediately take another sample. If the amount of 
acetylene is increasing, an active electrical arc is present within the 
transformer. It should be taken out of service. 
If you have a critical silicone (or mineral oil-filled transformer), such as a single 
station service transformer, or excitation transformer, you should find out if a 
spare is available at another facility or from Western Area Power Administration 
or Bonneville Power. If there are no other possible spares consider beginning the 
budget process for getting a spare transformer.

[Page 49] Several companies offer DGA computer software that 
diagnose transformer problems. These diagnoses must be used with engineering 
judgment and should never be taken at face value. The software is constantly 
changing. The Technical Service Center uses “ Transformer Oil Analyst” (TOA) by

One set of rules that TOA uses to generate alarms is based loosely on IEC 60599 
(table 6). These rules are also very useful in daily dissolved gas analysis. They 
are based on L1 limits of IEC 60599 except for acetylene. IEC 60599 gives a range 
for L1 limits instead of a specific value. TOA uses the average in this range and 
then gives the user a “heads up” if a generation rate exceeds 10% of L1 limits per 
month. Acetylene is the exception; IEEE sets an L1 limit of 35 ppm (too high), 
and IEC sets acetylene range at 3 to 50. TOA picks the lowest number (3 ppm) 
and sets the generation rate alarm value at 3 ppm per month.

The TDCG (Total Dissolved Combustible Gas) generation rate in ppm per day is calculated by dividing the change in TDCG by the number of days between samples when the transformer has been loaded. This method applies to both the total TDCG and the individual gas generation rates. The steps are as follows:

1. **Measure TDCG:** Take samples of the dissolved gases from the transformer at regular intervals.
2. **Record Data:** Record the TDCG values and the corresponding dates and times of the samples.
3. **Identify Change:** Determine if there has been a significant change in TDCG over a specific period.
4. **Calculate Generation Rate:** Divide the change in TDCG by the number of days between samples to get the TDCG generation rate in ppm per day.
5. **Individual Gas Rate:** Repeat the process for each individual gas to calculate its generation rate in ppm per day.

Note that "down-days" (days when the transformer is not loaded) should not be included in the calculation.

repeats.answer: If a DGA (Dissolved Gas Analysis) indicates a transformer problem, the first thing to do is **take another sample for comparison**. This is crucial because **mislabeling**, **contamination**, or **mishandling** during sampling or at the laboratory can occur, leading to false positives. By comparing the second sample with earlier DGAs, you can verify the presence of the problem. If the second sample shows similar increases in gases, then the issue is real, and further investigation is necessary.

Hot metal gases, specifically ethane (C2H6) and ethylene (C2H4), are sometimes called “hot metal gases.” These gases can indicate a problem inside the transformer, such as bad contacts on the tap changer or a bad connection somewhere in the circuit. [Page 49] Several companies offer DGA computer software that 
diagnose transformer problems. These diagnoses must be used with engineering

Gas Mixing. Concentration of gases in close proximity to an active fault will be 
higher than in the DGA oil sample. As distance increases from a fault, gas 
concentrations decrease. Equal mixing of dissolved gases in the total volume of oil 
depends on time and oil circulation. If there are no pumps to force oil through 
radiators, complete mixing of gases in the total oil volume takes longer. With 
pumping and normal loading, complete mixing equilibrium should be reached 
within 24 hours and will have little effect on DGA if an oil sample is taken 
24 hours or more after a problem begins.

ethylene, and ethane are reversed and vary inversely with temperature changes.

A Rogers Ratio is not reliable enough to base a decision on if:

* **Either gas used in the ratio is less than 10 times the detection limit of the gas chromatograph.** This is because the ratio method is only valid if a significant amount of the gases used in the ratio is present, and low gas levels can be influenced by instrument inaccuracies.
* **The transformer has an on-load tap changer and the amount of oil interchange between the tap changer tank and the main tank is not accounted for.** The manual mentions that this can lead to faulty readings not covered by the Rogers Ratio Method.
* **You don't have enough gas.** The Rogers Ratio Method relies on the presence of specific gases in the transformer oil. If the total combustible gas levels are low or the gas generation rate is not sufficient, the method may not provide a valid diagnosis. The manual suggests using the Key Gas Method to determine the presence of a problem based on total gas levels and key gas conditions.

Rogers Ratio Method, using three-key gas ratios, is based on earlier work by 
Doerneburg, who used five-key gas ratios. Ratio methods are only valid if a

The code 0 2 1 in the Rogers ratio table indicates a **Low energy partial discharge** fault.

Here’s a breakdown:

* **Code 0:** This indicates **No fault** or **Normal aging**.
* **Code 2:** This indicates **Low energy** discharges.
* **Code 1:** This indicates **Electric discharges in bubbles**, often caused by:
    * Insulation voids or super discharge gas saturation in oil.
    * Cavitation (from pumps) or high moisture in oil (water vapor bubbles).

The specific "Low energy partial discharge" fault is characterized by electric discharges in bubbles, often due to insulation voids or super discharge gas saturation in oil.

This code suggests potential issues with the transformer's insulation, which can lead to further problems if not addressed.

The CO2/CO ratio is used to interpret the health of cellulose insulation in a transformer. According to the manual, the CO2/CO ratio is considered a key indicator of potential paper involvement in electrical faults (arcing or sparking), along with some carbonization of paper. Here's how the ratio is interpreted:

- **Normal Ratio:** A normal CO2/CO ratio is typically around 7.
- **Probable Paper Involvement:** If the CO2/CO ratio is less than 3, it generally indicates probable paper involvement in an electrical fault.
- **Thermal Fault with Cellulose Involvement:** If the ratio is above 10, it suggests a thermal fault with the involvement of cellulose, provided there are no leaks within the transformer.

It's important to note that these interpretations are based on the assumption that the CO2 came from within the transformer, not from atmospheric leaks or contamination during sampling/lab handling. Additionally, the CO2/CO ratio can be influenced by normal aging and other sources, so subtracting the amount of CO and CO2 present before the sudden increase can help eliminate these variations when interpreting the results.

4.5 Moisture Problems 
Moisture, especially in the presence of oxygen, is extremely hazardous to transformer 
insulation. Each DGA and Doble test result should be examined carefully to see if 
water is increasing and to determine the moisture by dry weight (M/DW) or percent 
saturation that is in the paper insulation. When 2% M/DW is reached, plans should be 
made for a dry out. Never allow the M/DW to go above 2.5% in the paper or 30% oil 
saturation without drying out the transformer. Each time the moisture is doubled in a 
transformer, the life of the insulation is cut by one-half. Keep in mind that the life of 
the transformer is the life of the paper, and the purpose of the paper is to keep out 
moisture and oxygen. For service-aged transformers rated less than 69 kV, results of 
up to 35 ppm are considered acceptable. For 69 kV through 288 kV, the DGA test 
result of 25 ppm is considered acceptable. For greater than 288 kV, moisture should 
not exceed 20 ppm. However, the use of absolute values for water does not

However, there is also a recommendation for a more specific threshold of 70 ppm or more per month, which is based on the manual's reference to the IEEE limit of 3,000 ppm for CO content in a silicone transformer. This threshold suggests that if the CO content is increasing at a rate of 70 ppm or more per month, it may indicate a fault.

In addition, the CO2/CO ratio is also mentioned as an indicator of the involvement of cellulose degradation, with ratios less than 3 or greater than 10 being indicative of excessive cellulose degradation. However, this ratio alone is not sufficient to determine the presence of a fault.

Overall, the manual suggests that monitoring the rate of CO increase, along with other gas concentrations and ratios, can help indicate the presence of a fault in a transformer. However, the specific threshold for CO increase may vary depending on the type of transformer and the specific conditions.

The manual excerpt provides guidelines for determining the moisture content of paper insulation in transformers that necessitates a dry-out procedure. According to the information, the critical moisture levels are as follows:

- **2% M/DW (Moisture/Dry Weight)**: At this level, plans for a dry-out should be initiated.
- **Never exceed 2.5% M/DW in the paper or 30% oil saturation**: Exceeding these limits without performing a dry-out is not recommended.

The excerpt also mentions that each time the moisture in the transformer is doubled, the life of the insulation is halved. This emphasizes the importance of controlling moisture content to preserve the transformer's insulation.

Additionally, the manual suggests that decisions regarding dry-out should be based on trends observed over a period, considering multiple samples and oil temperature. It is crucial to avoid making decisions solely based on a single DGA result or calculation.

The ideal amount of oxygen inhibitor (DBPC) to be added when transformer oil is processed is 0.3% by total weight of the oil. This is based on the standard ASTM D-3487. If the inhibitor content is below 0.08%, the transformer is considered uninhibited, and the oxygen will attack the cellulose insulation. Conversely, if the inhibitor content drops below 0.1%, the transformer should be re-inhibited.

For example, if the transformer oil tested at 0.1%, you would need to add 0.2% of the total weight of the transformer oil to reach the ideal 0.3% level. If your transformer weighs 5,000 pounds of oil, you would need to add 10 pounds of DBPC (5,000 pounds * 0.002).

It's important to note that dissolving the inhibitor in the heated transformer oil may require some experimentation to achieve the correct dosage.

Oxidation of the insulation and oils forms acids as the transformer ages. The 
oxidation products form sludge and precipitate out inside the transformer. The 
acids attack metals inside the tank and form soaps (more sludge). Acid also 
attacks cellulose and accelerates insulation degradation. Sludging has been found 
to begin when the acid number reaches 0.40; it is obvious that the oil should be 
reclaimed before it reaches 0.40.  It is recommended that the oil be reclaimed 
when it reaches 0.20 mg KOH/gm [20]. As with all others, this decision must 
not be based on one DGA test, but watch for rising trend in the acid number each 
year. Plan ahead and begin budget planning before the acid number reaches 0.20.

repeats.answer:
According to the manual, to determine the percent saturation of oil holding 30 ppm of water at 40 °C, follow these steps:

1. Locate the 30 ppm water mark on the left line of Figure 20.
2. Draw a straight horizontal line from that point.
3. Draw a vertical line from the 40 °C temperature mark.
4. Find the point where the horizontal and vertical lines intersect.
5. Read the percent saturation value from the curve at the intersection point.

Based on Figure 20, the point of intersection falls approximately halfway between the 20% curve and the 30% curve. This suggests that the oil is approximately 25% saturated.

**Important Considerations:**

* **Temperature:** The percent saturation of water in oil is highly temperature-dependent. The manual warns that "Below 30 °C, the curves are not very accurate."
* **Trends:** A single DGA reading and calculation should not be the sole basis for a decision on dryout. The manual emphasizes the importance of monitoring trends over time and taking multiple samples for analysis.
* **Nomograph:** The nomograph in Figure 23 provides a quick check and can be used to verify the percent saturation calculation.
* **Insulation Degradation:** High moisture content (2.5% M/DW or more) and high percent saturation (30% or more) can accelerate insulation degradation.

**Recommendation:** If the DGA consistently shows 30 ppm water and the oil temperature is 40 °C, the oil is approximately 25% saturated. If concerns arise about insulation health, further analysis and potentially consultation with experts are recommended.

For a transformer rated 230 kV, the minimum acceptable dielectric breakdown voltage of the oil is **25 kV**. This is according to the manual's guidance on transformer oil tests, specifically as per Section 4.6.1 Dielectric Strength.

**Important Considerations:**

* This value is a minimum and should be considered alongside other test results and trends.
* The manual emphasizes that dielectric breakdown tests alone are not sufficient for assessing transformer health.
* Moisture, oxygen, and heat can compromise insulation long before dielectric breakdown occurs.
* Interfacial tension, water content, and other tests are crucial for a comprehensive assessment.

any decision on one test result, or on one type of test; instead, look at all the 
information over several DGAs and establish trends before making any decision.

repeats.answer: Good clean transformer oil should give an Interfacial Tension (IFT) number of **40 to 50 dynes per centimeter**. This value indicates a distinct line between the oil and distilled water, and is an excellent indicator of the oil's cleanliness and health.
repeats.context:

and paper insulation. These particles extend across the water/oil interface line 
and weaken the tension between the two liquids. The more particles, the weaker 
the interfacial tension and the lower the IFT number. The IFT and acid numbers 
together are an excellent indication of when the oil needs to be reclaimed. It is 
recommended the oil be reclaimed when the IFT number falls to 25 dynes per 
centimeter. At this level, the oil is very contaminated and must be reclaimed to 
prevent sludging, which begins around 22 dynes per centimeter. See FIST 3-5 
[20]. 
If oil is not reclaimed, sludge will settle on windings, insulation, etc., and cause 
loading and cooling problems discussed in an earlier section. This will greatly 
shorten transformer life.

The manual recommends reclaiming transformer oil when its Interfacial Tension (IFT) number falls to 25 dynes per centimeter, as this indicates significant contamination. Sludging, a critical issue that occurs when the oil becomes too contaminated, begins around 22 dynes per centimeter. The Acid Number is another key indicator of oil quality, and sludging is found to start when the Acid Number reaches 0.40 mg KOH/gm.

Additionally, the manual suggests reclaiming the oil when it reaches an Acid Number of 0.20 mg KOH/gm, emphasizing that this should be a trend observed over multiple years, not based on a single test. This is to ensure a well-informed decision-making process regarding oil reclamation.

To determine how much DBPC (Ditertiary Butyl Paracresol) should be added to a transformer holding 5,000 pounds of oil, follow these steps:

1. **Determine the ideal amount of DBPC:** According to the manual, the ideal amount of DBPC is 0.3% by the total weight of the oil. Given the transformer holds 5,000 pounds of oil, calculate 0.3% of 5,000 pounds.

2. **Calculate the amount of DBPC needed:** 
    - 0.3% of 5,000 pounds = (0.3 / 100) * 5,000 = 150 pounds.

3. **Consider the test result:** The transformer currently has 0.1% oxygen inhibitor. To reach the ideal 0.3% inhibitor level, you need to add a certain amount of DBPC to increase the inhibitor concentration from 0.1% to 0.3%.

4. **Calculate the additional DBPC needed:**
    - The amount of DBPC to add = (0.3% - 0.1%) of 5,000 pounds of oil.
    - (0.2 / 100) * 5,000 = 100 pounds of DBPC.

5. **Check the manual's instructions:** The manual states that you should dissolve 10 pounds of DBPC in the heated transformer oil. Therefore, you need to add 100 pounds of DBPC, which requires dissolving 10 pounds at a time.

6. **Perform the addition:** Add 10 pounds of DBPC to the heated oil until all 100 pounds are dissolved. Mix thoroughly and add this mixture to the transformer using the appropriate method from the transformer instruction manual.

Remember, if you add a little too much DBPC, it won't hurt the oil, but it's crucial to follow the manual's instructions and contact an experienced professional if needed.

You should not take an oil sample for DGA (Dissolved Gas Analysis) when:

1. The transformer is operating at or below freezing temperature. This is because water content in the oil can affect test values such as dielectric strength, power factor, and dissolved moisture content, leading to inaccurate results.

2. There is a negative pressure (vacuum) at the sample valve. This is a concern for all transformers, but conservator transformers are typically not affected. If the transformer is nitrogen blanketed, check the pressure/vacuum gauge. If the pressure is negative, it indicates a vacuum at the top of the transformer, and sampling should be avoided.

3. The transformer has developed a sudden increase in atmospheric gases, moisture, or hydrogen. In these cases, it is recommended to immediately take another sample to confirm the DGA values.

4. The transformer has a small leak in the sampling tubing or connections, which can draw air into the sample, leading to high atmospheric gas and moisture readings, or contamination with other particles.

5. The transformer operates at high ambient and oil temperatures with direct sun exposure on the side of the transformer tank where the sample valve is located, which can lead to the formation and accumulation of hydrogen in the sample valve and extension. This hydrogen will stay until a sample is drawn, leading to false hydrogen readings.

6. The transformer has been contaminated with hydrogen due to the galvanic action of dissimilar metals in the sample valve. If a galvanized or black iron pipe is installed in a brass valve, it can produce a thermocouple effect, leading to the generation of hydrogen in the void between the plug and valve gate.

7. The transformer shows an increase in acetylene generation, indicating an active electrical arc within the transformer. This requires immediate action, such as taking another sample and considering removing the transformer from service.
repeats.context:
[Page 72] 4.6.7 Taking Oil Samples for DGA.  Sampling procedures and lab handling are 
usually areas that cause the most problems in getting an accurate DGA. There 
are times when atmospheric gases, moisture, or hydrogen take a sudden leap from 
one DGA to the next. As has been mentioned, at these times, one should 
immediately take another sample to confirm DGA values. It is, of course, possible 
that the transformer has developed an atmospheric leak, or that a fault has 
suddenly occurred inside. More often, the sample has not been taken properly, or 
it has been contaminated with atmospheric gases or mishandled in other ways. 
The sample must be protected from all contamination, including atmospheric 
exposure. 
Do not take samples from the small sample ports located on the side of the large 
sample (drain) valves. These ports are too small to adequately flush the large 
valve and pipe nipple connected to the tank; in addition, air can be drawn past the 
threads and contaminate the sample. Fluid in the valve and pipe nipple remain 
dormant during operation and can be contaminated with moisture, microscopic 
stem packing particles, and other particles. The volume of oil in this location can 
also be contaminated with gases, especially hydrogen. Hydrogen is one of the 
easiest gasses to form. With hot sun on the side of the transformer tank where 
the sample valve is located, high ambient temperature, high oil temperature, and 
captured oil in the sample valve and extension, hydrogen formed will stay in this 

[Page 73] below. 
DGA Oil Sample Container.  Glass sample syringes are recommended. There 
are different containers such as stainless steel vacuum bottles and others. It is 
recommended that only glass syringes be used. If there is a small leak in the 
sampling tubing or connections, vacuum bottles will draw air into the sample, 
which cannot be seen inside the bottle. The sample will show high atmospheric 
gases and high moisture if the air is humid. Other contaminates such as 
suspended solids or free water cannot be seen inside the vacuum bottle. Glass 
syringes are the simplest to use because air bubbles are easily seen and expelled. 
Other contaminates are easily seen, and another sample can be immediately 
taken if the sample is contaminated. The downside is that glass syringes must be 
handled carefully and must be protected from direct sunlight. They should be 
returned to their shipping container immediately after taking a sample. If they 
are exposed to sunlight for any time, hydrogen will be generated and the DGA will 
show false hydrogen readings. 
For these reasons, glass syringes are recommended, and the instructions below 
include only this sampling method. 
Obtain a brass pipe plug (normally 2 inches) that will thread into the sample 
valve at the bottom of the transformer. Drill and tap the pipe plug for F-inch 
NPT and insert a F-inch pipe nipple (brass if possible) and attach a small F-inch 
valve for controlling the sample flow. Attach a F-inch tygon tubing adaptor to the 
small valve outlet. 

[Page 49] Several companies offer DGA computer software that 
diagnose transformer problems. These diagnoses must be used with engineering

To determine how much oil head corresponds to one psi of pressure at a transformer sample valve, we need to consider the information provided in the manual. 

According to the manual, on Page 73, it states that "head is about 2.9 feet (2 feet 10.8 inches) of oil per pounds per square inch (psi)." This can be expressed as:

Head (in feet) = 2.9 feet/psi

To convert this to a more common unit of measurement, such as inches, we can multiply by 12 (since there are 12 inches in a foot):

Head (in inches) = 2.9 feet/psi * 12 inches/foot = 34.8 inches/psi

Therefore, for every one psi of pressure at a transformer sample valve, there is approximately 34.8 inches of oil head.

Based on the manual excerpts, here's how to fill a glass syringe when taking a DGA oil sample:

1. **Fill the syringe partially:**
   - After allowing a small amount (about 10 cubic centimeters or cc) of oil to flow into the syringe from the waste bucket, don't eject all the oil. Leave 1-2 cc of oil in the syringe. This prevents air bubbles from reentering the syringe.

2. **Avoid pulling the syringe handle:**
   - When taking the sample, don't pull the syringe handle (piston) directly. This creates a vacuum and can lead to air bubbles forming. Instead, carefully control the movement of the piston using your hand to ensure slow and deliberate movement.

3. **Minimize air bubbles:**
   - Carefully press the syringe piston to eject any remaining air bubbles. Make sure you leave a small amount of oil in the syringe to ensure the sample isn't contaminated.

4. **Handle with care:**
   - Glass syringes require careful handling. They should be protected from direct sunlight, as exposure can lead to hydrogen generation and false DGA readings. Always return the syringe to its shipping container immediately after taking a sample.

Remember, these instructions emphasize the use of glass syringes for DGA oil sampling due to their advantages in visibility and simplicity.

According to the manual, a furan analysis with the annual DGA (Dissolved Gas Analysis) is recommended for silicone oil-filled transformers when:

1. The CO (carbon monoxide) content exceeds the IEEE limit of 3,000 ppm.
2. The generation rate G1 (Generation Rate 1) is met or exceeded.

These criteria are specifically mentioned in the context of a silicone oil-filled transformer, where the CO generation rate may be masked by the normal production of CO from the silicone oil itself. A furan analysis can help determine if the paper insulation is involved in the fault by indicating if the paper is being heated. 

Additionally, if the DGA shows an increase in other fault gases besides CO, a furan analysis can help distinguish between CO from paper degradation and CO from normal aging of the oil.

To calculate the generation rate per day from the silicone transformer gas limits given per month, you can follow these steps:

1. Take the generation rate per month (G1 or G2) as given in the table.
2. Divide the generation rate per month by 30 to get the generation rate per day.

For example, if G1 is 100 ppm per month for hydrogen, you would divide 100 by 30 to get approximately 3.33 ppm per day.

Remember that this calculation assumes a consistent generation rate throughout the month. If the generation rate varies, you may need to adjust the calculation accordingly.

Transformers are so complex that it is impossible to put all symptoms and causes 
into a chart. Several additional transformer problems are listed below; there are 
many others. 
1. Gases are generated by normal operation and aging, mostly H2 and CO with 
some CH4. 
2. Operating transformers at sustained overload will generate combustible gases. 
3. Problems with cooling systems, discussed in an earlier section, can cause 
overheating. 
4. A blocked oil duct inside the transformer can cause local overheating, 
generating gases. 
5. An oil directing baffle loose inside the transformer causes mis-direction of 
cooling oil. 
6. Oil circulating pump problems (bearing wear, impeller loose or worn) can cause 
transformer cooling problems. 
7. Oil level is too low; this will not be obvious if the level indicator is inoperative.

The manual provides specific guidelines for comparing winding resistances between phases or with factory values. According to the manual, a satisfactory agreement is within 5% for any of the comparisons mentioned (phase resistances, wye connected transformers, delta-connected windings, or factory measurements).

Regarding the temperature correction for copper windings, the manual specifies a constant of 234.5 °C for copper. This constant (Tk) is used in the formula mentioned on Page 82, which is:

Rs = Rm * (Tm + Tk) / (Tm + Ts)

Where:
- Rs is the resistance at the factory reference temperature
- Rm is the resistance you actually measured
- Tm is the temperature at which you took the measurements
- Tk is the temperature constant for the metal (234.5 °C for copper)
- Ts is the factory reference temperature (usually 75 °C)

This formula allows you to convert your resistance measurements to the factory reference temperature and ensure accurate comparisons.
repeats.context:
[Page 83] It is very difficult to determine actual winding temperature in the field, 
and, normally, this is not needed. You only need to do the above temperature 
corrections if you are going to compare resistances to factory values. Normally, 
only the phase resistances are compared to each other, and you do not need the 
winding temperature to compare individual windings. 
You can compare winding resistances to factory values; change in these values can 
reveal serious problems. A suggested method to obtain an accurate temperature 
is outlined below. If a transformer has just been de-energized for testing, the 
winding will be cooler on the bottom than the top, and the winding hot spot will be 
hotter than the top oil temperature. What is needed is the average winding 
temperature, and it is important to get the temperature as accurate as possible for 
comparisons. 
The most accurate method is to allow the transformer sit de-energized until 
temperatures are equalized. This test can reveal serious problems, so it’s worth 
the effort.

above and using a micro-ohmmeter or Kelvin Bridge for values under 1 ohm.

quick and easy to use. Take readings from the top of each bushing to neutral for 
wye connected windings and across each pair of bushings for delta connected 
windings. If the neutral bushing is not available on wye connected windings, you 
can take each one

According to the manual excerpts, the expected readings for a core insulation resistance test are as follows:

* A new transformer should read greater than 1,000 megohms.
* A service-aged transformer should read greater than 100 megohms.
* Readings between 10 and 100 megohms are indicative of deteriorating insulation between the core and ground.
* Readings less than 10 megohms are cause for investigation, as they may indicate a problem with the insulation.

Note that this test is only necessary if the winding resistance test above shows all the connections and if tap changer contacts are in good condition.

can take each one to ground (if the neutral is grounded), or take readings between 
pairs of bushings as if it were a delta winding. Be consistent each time so that a

insulation resistance and inadvertent core ground test is used if an additional core 
ground is suspected; this may be indicated by the DGA. Key gases to look for are

there is a poor connection at the bottom of a bushing or a bad tap changer contact. 
Therefore, this test is only necessary if the winding resistance test above shows all 
the connections and if tap changer contacts are in good condition. 
The intentional core ground must be disconnected. This may be difficult, and 
some oil may have to be drained to accomplish this. On some transformers, core 
grounds are brought outside through insulated bushings and are easily accessed.

4.7 Transformer Testing 
When the transformer is new before energizing and every 3 to 5 years, the 
transformer and bushings should be Doble tested.  Transformer testing falls into 
three broad categories: Factory testing when the transformer is new or has been 
refurbished, acceptance testing upon delivery, and field testing for maintenance and 
diagnostic purposes. Some tests at the factory are common to most power 
transformers, but many of the factory tests are transformer- specific. Table 17 lists 
several tests. This test chart has been adapted from IEEE 62-1995 reference [19]. Not 
all of the listed tests are done at the factory, and not all of them are done in the field. 
Each transformer and each situation is different, requiring its own unique approach 
and tests. 
Details of how to run specific tests will not be addressed in this FIST. It would be 
impractical to repeat how to do Doble testing of a transformer when the information is 
readily available in Doble publications. With some exceptions, this is true for most of 
the tests. Specific information is readily available within the test instrument 
manufacturers literature. Another example is the transformer turns ratio test (TTR); 
specific test information is available with the instrument. However, information on 
some tests may not be available and will be covered briefly.

3.1 Dry Type Transformers 
Cooling classes of dry type transformers are covered by ANSI/IEEE standard 
C57.12.01 Section 5.1 [1]. A short explanation of each class is given below. 
1. Class AA are ventilated, self-cooled transformers. This means that there are 
ventilation ports located in outside walls of the transformer enclosure. There are no 
fans to force air into and out of the enclosure with typically no external fins or 
radiators. Cooler air enters the lower ports, is heated as it rises past windings, and 
exits the upper ventilation ports. (It will not be repeated below; but it is obvious that 
in every cooling class, some heat is also removed by natural circulation of air around 
the outside of the enclosure.) 
2. Class AFA transformers are self-cooled (A) and additionally cooled by forced 
circulation of air (FA). This means that there are ventilation ports for fan inlets and 
outlets only. (Inlets are usually filtered.) Normally, there are no additional 
ventilation ports for natural air circulation. 
3. Class AA/FA transformers are ventilated, self-cooled (same as Class AA in item 1). 
In addition, they have a fan or fans providing additional forced-air cooling. Fans may 
be wired to start automatically when the temperature reaches a pre-set

3. Class AA/FA transformers are ventilated, self-cooled (same as Class AA in item 1). 
In addition, they have a fan or fans providing additional forced-air cooling. Fans may 
be wired to start automatically when the temperature reaches a pre-set value. These 
transformers generally have a dual load rating, one for AA (self-cooling natural air 
flow) and a larger load rating for FA (forced air flow). 
4. Class ANV transformers are self-cooled (A), non-ventilated (NV) units. The 
enclosure has no ventilation ports or fans and is not sealed to exclude migration of 
outside air, but there are no provisions to intentionally allow outside air to enter and 
exit. Cooling is by natural circulation of air around the enclosure. This transformer 
may have some type of fins attached outside the enclosure to increase surface area for 
additional cooling. 
5. Class GA transformers are sealed with a gas inside (G) and are self-cooled (A). The 
enclosure is hermetically sealed to prevent leakage. These transformers typically have 
a gas, such as nitrogen or freon, to provide high dielectric and good heat removal. 
Cooling occurs by natural circulation of air around the outside of the enclosure. There 
are no fans to circulate cooling air; however, there may be fins attached to the outside 
to aid in cooling.

The manual does not provide a specific replacement frequency for the nitrogen cylinder in a gas-blanketed transformer. However, it does mention the importance of testing the pressure relief function of the nitrogen blanketed transformer every year and replacing the pressure relief device if it is 30 years old. Additionally, it recommends testing the alarm circuits and examining the top of the transformer tank around the pressure relief device every 3 to 5 years during other maintenance or testing.

If the nitrogen cylinder is part of the pressure relief device, it may need to be replaced if the device is 30 years old or if it is leaking. However, the manual does not provide specific guidelines for replacing the nitrogen cylinder independently.

In summary, while the manual does not provide a specific replacement frequency for the nitrogen cylinder, it emphasizes the importance of testing and maintaining the pressure relief function of the nitrogen blanketed transformer on a regular basis. If the cylinder is part of the pressure relief device, it may need to be replaced if the device is 30 years old or if it is leaking.

repeats.answer: According to Reclamation's equipment-life studies, the average life of a Reclamation transformer is 40 years. This estimate is based on the assumption that transformers receive adequate maintenance over their service life, operate at lower ambient temperatures and with lower loads, and are continuously operated at rated load and service conditions.

This document is to provide guidance to Bureau of Reclamation (Reclamation) powerplant 
personnel in maintenance, diagnostics, and testing of transformers and associated 
equipment. 
2. INTRODUCTION TO RECLAMATION TRANSFORMERS 
Transformers rated 500 kilovoltamperes (kVA) and above are considered power 
transformers. Reclamation has hundreds of power transformers with voltages as low as 
480 volts (V) and as high as 550 kilovolts (kV). 
All generator step-up (GSU) transformers, and many station service, and excitation 
transformers are considered power transformers because they are rated 500 kVA or larger. 
Standards organizations such as American National Standards Institute/Institute of 
Electrical and Electronic Engineers (ANSI/IEEE) consider average GSU transformer life to 
be 20 to 25 years. This estimate is based on continuous operation at rated load and service 
conditions with an average ambient temperature of 40 °C (104 °F) and a temperature rise 
of 65 °C. This estimate is also based on the assumption that transformers receive adequate 
maintenance over their service life [24]. Reclamation, Bonneville Power Administration, 
and Western Area Power Administration conduct regular studies to determine statistical 
equipment life. These studies show that average life of a Reclamation transformer is 
40 years. Reclamation gets longer service than IEEE estimates because we operate at 
lower ambient temperatures and with lower loads. A significant number of transformers 
were purchased in the 1940s, 1950s, and into the 1970s. Several have been replaced, but

The manual states that operating a transformer only 10 °C above its rating will cut transformer life by 50%. This is a critical piece of information for maintaining the longevity of transformers, especially those that are older or critical to the generation process.

To ensure that transformers are running within the recommended parameters, it is important to monitor their temperature and cooling systems. The manual also emphasizes the importance of accurate diagnostics and high-quality maintenance, particularly for older transformers.

In addition to monitoring temperature, it is also crucial to regularly inspect and test oil level indicators to ensure that they are functioning correctly. This can help prevent premature failure and ensure that the transformer is operating safely and efficiently.

Current minimum replacement time is around 14 months; a more realistic time may be

transformers, but absolutely essential for older ones—especially for critical transformers 
that would cause loss of generation. It is also very important to consider providing spares 
for critical transformers. 
3. TRANSFORMER COOLING METHODS 
Heat is one of the most common destroyers of transformers. Operation at only 10 °C above 
the transformer rating will cut transformer life by 50%. Heat is caused by internal losses 
due to loading, high ambient temperature, and solar radiation. It is important to under­
stand how your particular transformers are cooled and how to detect problems in the 
cooling systems. ANSI and IEEE require the cooling class of each transformer to appear on 
its nameplate. Cooling classifications, with short explanations, appear in sections 3.1 and 
3.2. The letters of the class designate inside atmosphere and type or types of cooling. In 
some transformers, more than one class of cooling and load rating are indicated. At each

For a dry type transformer, cooling class ANV indicates that the unit is self-cooled (A) and non-ventilated (NV). This means that the transformer relies on natural circulation of air around the enclosure for cooling, without the use of ventilation ports or fans. The enclosure is not sealed to exclude outside air, but it does not have provisions to allow air to enter and exit intentionally.

Natural circulation occurs because of the temperature differences within the transformer. As the windings heat up, the air naturally circulates around the enclosure, cooling it. To further enhance cooling, the transformer may have fins attached to the outside to increase the surface area exposed to the air.

3.1 Dry Type Transformers 
Cooling classes of dry type transformers are covered by ANSI/IEEE standard 
C57.12.01 Section 5.1 [1]. A short explanation of each class is given below. 
1. Class AA are ventilated, self-cooled transformers. This means that there are 
ventilation ports located in outside walls of the transformer enclosure. There are no 
fans to force air into and out of the enclosure with typically no external fins or 
radiators. Cooler air enters the lower ports, is heated as it rises past windings, and 
exits the upper ventilation ports. (It will not be repeated below; but it is obvious that 
in every cooling class, some heat is also removed by natural circulation of air around 
the outside of the enclosure.) 
2. Class AFA transformers are self-cooled (A) and additionally cooled by forced 
circulation of air (FA). This means that there are ventilation ports for fan inlets and 
outlets only. (Inlets are usually filtered.) Normally, there are no additional 
ventilation ports for natural air circulation. 
3. Class AA/FA transformers are ventilated, self-cooled (same as Class AA in item 1). 
In addition, they have a fan or fans providing additional forced-air cooling. Fans may 
be wired to start automatically when the temperature reaches a pre-set

classes. 
1. Class FOA: Liquid-immersed, forced liquid-cooled with forced air-cooled. This 
transformer normally has only one rating. The transformer is cooled by pumping 
oil (forced oil) through a radiator normally attached to the outside of the tank. 
Also, air is forced by fans over the cooling surface. 
2. Class FOW: Liquid-immersed, forced liquid-cooled, water cooled. This 
transformer is cooled by an oil/water heat exchanger normally mounted separately 
from the tank. Both the transformer oil and the cooling water are pumped 
(forced) through the heat exchanger to accomplish cooling.

3. Class AA/FA transformers are ventilated, self-cooled (same as Class AA in item 1). 
In addition, they have a fan or fans providing additional forced-air cooling. Fans may 
be wired to start automatically when the temperature reaches a pre-set value. These 
transformers generally have a dual load rating, one for AA (self-cooling natural air 
flow) and a larger load rating for FA (forced air flow). 
4. Class ANV transformers are self-cooled (A), non-ventilated (NV) units. The 
enclosure has no ventilation ports or fans and is not sealed to exclude migration of 
outside air, but there are no provisions to intentionally allow outside air to enter and 
exit. Cooling is by natural circulation of air around the enclosure. This transformer 
may have some type of fins attached outside the enclosure to increase surface area for 
additional cooling. 
5. Class GA transformers are sealed with a gas inside (G) and are self-cooled (A). The 
enclosure is hermetically sealed to prevent leakage. These transformers typically have 
a gas, such as nitrogen or freon, to provide high dielectric and good heat removal. 
Cooling occurs by natural circulation of air around the outside of the enclosure. There 
are no fans to circulate cooling air; however, there may be fins attached to the outside 
to aid in cooling.

The nitrogen-blanketed transformer should be maintained with a nitrogen pressure of 2.5 to 3 psi to ensure that moist air will not be pulled in. This is achieved by adding nitrogen to the system to reach this pressure range. Additionally, the nitrogen pressure should be checked against the weekly data sheets, and if the pressure never varies with seasonal temperature changes, the gage is considered defective. It's crucial to monitor the pressure gage regularly to prevent any issues.

For the pressurized inert gas sealed system, the pressure is maintained by a nitrogen gas bottle with a regulated pressure between 0.5 and 5 psi. This system is specifically designed to keep the space above the oil pressurized with a dry inert gas, preventing air and moisture from coming into contact with the insulating oil. The pressure gages are positioned for both high and low pressures, ensuring proper monitoring of the system.

Water should not be sprayed on transformer radiators to increase cooling for the following reasons:

1. **Mineral Deposits:** The manual explicitly warns against using water to increase cooling due to the potential for mineral deposits. These deposits can form on the radiators as water evaporates and are difficult to remove. As a result, the cooling efficiency will decrease further.

2. **Oil Contamination:** If the transformer has an oil leak, spraying water on the radiators could cause oil to mix with the water, leading to contamination. This contamination can affect the transformer's performance and safety.

3. **Safety Hazards:** Spraying water on a transformer, especially when it is already running, can lead to electrical hazards. Water can disrupt the transformer's internal workings and potentially cause short circuits or damage to sensitive components.

4. **Alternative Methods Recommended:** The manual suggests other methods to increase cooling, such as adding additional fans or using portable fans. These methods are considered safer and more effective in maintaining optimal transformer temperatures.

In summary, while water may provide temporary cooling, it is not a recommended or safe method to increase transformer cooling due to the potential risks of mineral deposits, oil contamination, and safety hazards.

To correct a three-phase oil pump that is running backwards, you should follow these steps according to the manual:

1. **Check for Reverse Rotation**: If you suspect the pump is running backwards, the best indication is usually the pump being very noisy and the motor load current being lower than for full load. Check the pump for proper rotation by reversing two-phase leads if necessary.

2. **Inspect Oil Flow Indicator**: The oil flow indicator, which has a small paddle that extends into the oil stream, can provide valuable information. If the flow is too low, the flag will rotate. However, if there is no flow, a spring returns the flag to the off position, and a switch provides an alarm. Ensure the alarm point activates when the pump stops, and check the pointer's position when the pump is off and running.

3. **Check Oil Flow with Ultrasonic Flow Meter**: An ultrasonic flow meter can detect worn bearings, rubbing impellers, and other unusual noises. This method can help identify specific issues with the pump.

4. **Inspect Piping and Connections**: Check the piping and connections for leaks. Ensure all valves are fully open and inspect the pump impellers to ensure they are secure on the shaft.

5. **Check Motor Load Current**: If the motor load current is low, it may indicate low oil flow. Carefully inspect all valves and check for sludge buildup or debris in lines that could be causing the issue.

6. **Monitor Motor Load Current and Listen for Noises**: If the motor load current is high, it could indicate impeded pump rotation. Listen for unusual noises, as thrust bearing wear can cause the impeller to advance on the housing.

7. **Regular Maintenance**: After one month of service and yearly, inspect and test the oil pumps. Adjust the temperature controller to ensure all fans are running, and listen for unusual noises from fan bearings and loose blades. Use an IR scan to detect bad bearings if the fans are running. Regularly check the oil flow indicator and ensure it is functioning correctly.

If the device has operated, about 2 inches of the colored rod will be visible. If the top contacts of a Buchholz relay activate during operation, it means that the transformer is gassing, and the oil level is very low. On the other hand, if the bottom contacts activate, it means that the oil level is very low, or a pressure wave has activated, causing the oil to be displaced and the bottom float to descend. 

In both cases, the transformer should not be re-energized until the exact cause of the activation has been determined and corrected.

Old style sudden pressure relays have only one bellows. A sudden excessive
